title: Explaining it
hook: scholars explain verses by other verses, hadith, language and context

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pickthall and the translation of 1934: two Muslims, two temperaments. Your line was two voices one line. Did you hear out someone who saw it differently? Day three hundred twenty-one.

A verse says that those who believe, and don't mix their belief with wrongdoing, are the ones who will be safe. When the companions heard it, they were frightened. Which of us, they asked, has never done wrong? If that's the condition, who is safe? They took the question straight to the Prophet ﷺ. His answer didn't come out of nowhere. He pointed them to another verse. Today: explaining it.
screen: `WHICH OF US HAS NEVER DONE WRONG?` → `THEY TOOK IT TO THE PROPHET.` → `HE POINTED TO ANOTHER VERSE.`

segments.voice: The Prophet told them: it isn't what you think. Haven't you heard what Luqman said to his son? And he recited from Surah 31, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong." The wrong meant in the first verse was that one: setting up partners with God, not every everyday failing. The companions could breathe again. That story, in Bukhari, is the seed of tafsir, explaining the Qur'an. The word comes from a root meaning to uncover, to lay open. And scholars have climbed the same ladder ever since. First, the Qur'an explains the Qur'an: one verse opens another, as Luqman's line opened the first. Second, the Prophet's words and example, the hadith. Third, the understanding of the companions who were there, like Ibn Abbas, for whom the Prophet prayed that he be given understanding of the religion. Fourth, the Arabic language itself: grammar, rare words, even old Arabic poetry, which Ibn Abbas is reported to have used to explain unusual words. And context: the occasions of revelation you met eleven days ago. From these came the great written commentaries. Al-Tabari, in the tenth century, gathered the early reports verse by verse into a huge work. Ibn Kathir, in the fourteenth, wrote one of the most read commentaries, and it still is. Others focus on law, or language, or the inner meanings the Sufis looked for. And scholars warn against explaining the Qur'an by personal opinion alone, without knowledge. Tafsir isn't a way of adding to the book. It's a way of listening to it more closely, letting its own verses, and the people nearest to it, speak first.
screen: `LUQMAN'S LINE OPENS THE VERSE` · `THE QUR'AN EXPLAINS THE QUR'AN` · `HADITH, COMPANIONS, LANGUAGE` · `AL-TABARI AND IBN KATHIR`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one tafsir note. After the bell, you might look up a short commentary on al-Ikhlas or al-Asr; Ibn Kathir's is easy to find in English. For now, try the first rung of the ladder. Hold one verse you know, maybe with hardship goeth ease, and ask: where else in the Qur'an have I heard this idea? Let another verse come to mind, or just let the question sit. The bell holds the time.
Tafsir. Explaining the Qur'an, from a root meaning to uncover: by the Qur'an itself, the hadith, the companions and the language. Today's word.

Your line: the book explains itself. Today, when something someone says puzzles you, before deciding what they meant, look at what else they've said. Let them explain themselves. Day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims read tafsir, commentary on the Qur'an, in study circles, in Friday sermons and at home; classic commentaries like those of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir are widely read and translated.
